content:
**False premise.**

In Switzerland, if a popular initiative is accepted by the people in a referendum, it becomes part of the Federal Constitution. Neither the Federal Council nor the Federal Assembly (parliament) has the authority to reject or prevent its implementation.  
However, it is possible for the Federal Assembly to propose a **counter-proposal**. If both the popular initiative and the counter-proposal are submitted to a popular vote and one of them is accepted, it replaces the other. But they cannot simply reject the initiative.  
If a popular initiative conflicts with international law or is unconstitutional, the Federal Council may ask the Federal Supreme Court to rule on its validity before it is put to a vote — but even then, the court decides; the authorities do not have the power to reject it outright after it has passed the popular vote.

So, strictly speaking, no — the parliament or the Federal Council **cannot** reject a popular initiative that has been accepted by the people.
